title: Bump Values Until Strictly Rising
statement:
You get an integer array nums. One operation picks any element and adds 1 to it. Values can only go up.

Return the fewest operations needed to make the array strictly increasing: every element must be greater than the one before it. An array with one element already counts as strictly increasing.

examples.why: Raise the second 3 to 4 (1 operation) and the third to 5 (2 operations).
The 2 must become 6 (4 operations). Then the 4 must beat the new 6, not the old 2: it becomes 7 (3 operations).

hints: The first element never needs to change. Why would raising it ever help?
Walk left to right. Each element must be at least one more than the final value of the element before it.
If nums[i] ≤ prev, raise it to prev + 1 and add the difference. Raising it any higher only costs more now and makes later elements cost more too.

explain.intuition:
Raising a value makes everything after it harder, so each value should end as low as possible. The first value stays as it is. Every later value must end at least at prev + 1, where prev is the final value of its left neighbour. If it is already above that, leave it; otherwise raise it to exactly prev + 1.

This greedy choice is safe because a lower final value never hurts later elements: the right side only needs to beat whatever we leave behind.
steps: For each later v: if v > prev, set prev = v.
Otherwise add prev + 1 − v to ops and set prev = prev + 1.
pitfalls: Comparing with the original left neighbour instead of its raised value. In [1, 5, 2, 4] the 4 must beat 6, not 2.
Making the array non-decreasing instead of strictly increasing: equal neighbours still cost one operation.
Using a 32-bit counter in another language. The total can reach about 5·10⁹.

solutions.title: Add one at a time
solutions.idea: Simulate the operations: keep adding 1 to an element while it does not beat its left neighbour.

solutions.title: Greedy: raise to exactly prev + 1
solutions.idea: Each element ends at max(itself, prev + 1); the gap is the cost.

followups: Operations may also subtract 1. What is the fewest total change now? (Hint: think about nums[i] − i.)
Return the final array as well. Does anything change in the algorithm?
lcTitle: Minimum Operations to Make the Array Increasing
